title: Ingestion: clean before you index
subtitle: Headers, broken words and repeated lines: the junk that spoils RAG
mission: Aurora’s handbook came out of a PDF. Before any embedding, clean the text: drop headers and footers, join broken words and remove repeated lines. Then check that search finds the answer.

predict.question: the raw text has 12 lines. How many are junk (header, footer or repeated)?

feedback.right: right: 4 header and footer lines and 1 repeated, almost half the text. In a 300-page PDF that’s hundreds of useless chunks in the index.
feedback.wrong: it’s 5: 4 header and footer lines and 1 repeated. A PDF stores the page layout, not flowing text; the junk comes along.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Turn off all three clean-ups and count what shows up in red.

coach.ui: guess noted. Turn off all three switches to see the raw text; then turn them on one at a time.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run clean --headers no --hyphen no --dupes no, then turn them on one at a time.

tryNext.ui: Now ask "Can I split my vacation?" with and without removing dupes. Search finds it both ways, but the index gets bigger.
tryNext.cmd: Run clean "Can I split my vacation?" --dupes no and compare the lines.

why.simples:
Before storing a document for the AI to look up, we tidy the mess: drop the "header on every page", glue back words the PDF split at line ends and throw away repeats.
If "ad-" and "vance" stay apart, nobody finds "advance".
why.dev:
Ingestion is extract, clean and normalize before chunking. Typical rules: drop headers and footers by pattern (text repeated on every page), join end-of-line hyphenation, remove exact duplicates, normalize whitespace and Unicode.
Keep useful metadata (section, page, date) apart from the text: it’s for filtering and citing, not for embedding.
why.especialista:
PDF extraction is RAG’s most fragile part: tables become scrambled text, columns mix, scanned PDFs need OCR. Measure quality on samples (how many chunks have broken words or junk) before blaming the embedding model.
Near-duplicates (versions of the same document) need similarity dedup and a "current version" rule; otherwise the assistant cites the old policy. Reprocess when the source changes and version the pipeline.

mission.ui: time to break it: turn off "Join broken words" and ask how far in advance to request vacation.
mission.cmd: time to break it: run clean "How far in advance do I request vacation?" --hyphen no

break.success: Broken: with {broken} split word, "advance" doesn’t exist in the index and search returned another line. One end-of-line hyphen was enough to hide the answer.
break.calm: {removed} junk lines removed and the answer was found. To break it, leave the word split and ask about advance notice.

ui: Pick a question and flip the switches; the scene updates by itself.
Lines with "!" are headers or footers; "split words" are the ones the PDF broke with a hyphen.
Turn off "Join broken words" with the advance-notice question.
cmd: The question goes in quotes, after clean. Clean-ups start on.
clean "How far in advance do I request vacation?" --hyphen no

steps: Take a real PDF from your company (handbook, policy) and extract the text with a tool like pdftotext or the pypdf library.
Look for three problems: lines repeated on every page, words split with an end-of-line hyphen and duplicated paragraphs.
Write one rule for each and count how many lines remain.
recipe.ok: the clean text has no repeated header or split word, and a search for a word that used to be split (like "advance") finds the right paragraph.
